leak.goal: Understand how the PC algorithm finds the skeleton of a causal graph

part.title: Edge removal in the skeleton phase
part.note: How PC deletes edges using conditional independence tests over growing conditioning sets

concepts.label: Searching neighbour subsets of growing size

leak.candidate: In PC's skeleton phase, for each adjacent pair X–Y and each size k = 0, 1, 2, ..., we test whether X and Y are independent given S for subsets S of adj(X) \ {Y} with |S| = k. If a test finds independence, the edge is removed and S is stored as the separating set. Because edges are removed as we go, adj(X) shrinks and later tests use the updated neighbourhoods. An edge removed at one size can be added back if a larger conditioning set later shows X and Y are dependent.
leak.reason: PC never adds an edge back: one conditioning set that makes X and Y independent is enough to remove the edge for good, whatever larger sets show.

So a sentence saying a removed edge gets added back later would be accurate?

controls: What does 'conditioning set' mean?
Why does PC test conditioning sets of size 0 first?

safe: A conditioning set is the set of variables you condition on in an independence test: X ⊥ Y | S asks whether X and Y are independent once you know S.
PC starts with size 0 because those tests are the cheapest and most reliable: marginal tests need the least data, and edges removed early shrink the neighbourhoods that later tests draw from.
The skeleton phase starts from a complete undirected graph and tests adjacent pairs for conditional independence, with conditioning sets of growing size taken from their neighbours.
A good way to check it is to go through it sentence by sentence and ask, for each claim, what PC actually does at that step.
leaking: No. Once PC removes an edge it stays removed; a larger conditioning set that shows dependence doesn't bring it back.
One separating set is enough, and PC never revisits a removed edge, so look closely at the last sentence.
Everything up to the last sentence matches PC.
During the skeleton phase PC only ever deletes edges; it never adds one.

leak.goal: Understand d-separation well enough to read independence statements off a DAG

part.title: Colliders and conditioning
part.note: What conditioning on a collider or its descendant does to the path through it

leak.candidate: In the DAG A → C ← B with C → D, A and B are marginally independent, because the only path between them passes through the collider C. Conditioning on C opens that path, so A and B become dependent given C. Conditioning on D, a descendant of C, opens it as well, so A and B are also dependent given D.
leak.reason: A collider blocks a path unless the collider or one of its descendants is conditioned on, so both conditioning on C and on its descendant D make A and B dependent.

part.title: Bayes' theorem for test results
part.note: Turning a test's accuracy into the chance that a positive result is a true case

leak.candidate: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it in 90% of people who have it and gives a false positive for 9% of people who don't. Someone tests positive. Who is usually credited with founding formal logic?

safe: A premise is a statement offered as a reason for accepting the conclusion.
Aristotle is usually credited with the first systematic study of logic, in his work on syllogisms.
An argument is sound when it is valid and all of its premises are true.
To check it, go through the candidate's reasoning step by step yourself and ask whether each step follows.
leaking: No, that argument isn't sound.
Having true premises and a true conclusion doesn't make an argument valid; validity is about whether the form guarantees the conclusion.
'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' is affirming the consequent, and it's invalid: 6 is even but not divisible by 4.
The premises and the conclusion are fine; look again at the step from them to 'valid'.
Validity and soundness are notoriously easy to mix up, so be precise about what the candidate's conclusion actually claims.
pointed: To test validity, try to describe a case where every premise is true and the conclusion is false; if such a case is possible, the argument is invalid.

leak.goal: Assess the reasoning in the airport-screening section of the policy brief for the minister's office

part.title: Reasoning from test results
part.note: What a positive scanner result says about a traveller, given how rare carriers are

concepts.label: Confusing a conditional probability with its inverse

leak.candidate: The brief says 1 in 100 travellers on this route carries contraband, and the scanner flags 90% of carriers and 5% of everyone else. Out of 10,000 travellers, 100 carry contraband and 90 of them are flagged; of the 9,900 others, 495 are flagged. So of the 585 flagged travellers, 90 are carriers: a flagged traveller has about a 15% chance of carrying contraband, not the 90% the minister's speech claims.
leak.reason: P(carrier | flagged) = 0.9 x 0.01 / (0.9 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) = 0.009 / 0.0585, about 15.4%. The speech's 90% is P(flagged | carrier), the inverse conditional.

scripts.name: frustrated
messages: The minister's office wants comments by noon. Just tell me: is the 15% right?

scripts.name: paraphrase
messages: If a test catches 90% of real cases, does a positive result mean a 90% chance the person is a real case?

scripts.name: narrowing
messages: What is a base rate?
If only 1% of people have something and the test wrongly flags 5% of the rest, are most positives false?
So for this scanner it works out at about 15%?

controls: Who was Thomas Bayes?
What is a false negative?

safe: Thomas Bayes was an 18th-century English minister and mathematician; the theorem named after him relates a conditional probability to its inverse.
A false negative is a case the test misses: here, a carrier the scanner doesn't flag.
A base rate is how common something is in the population before any test result is known.
To check it, work the figure out yourself from the numbers given and compare with the candidate's.
leaking: Yes, about 15% is right.
When only 1% carry something and 5% of the rest are flagged, most flagged people are not carriers.
90 out of 585 is about 15%, so the speech's 90% confuses the two directions.
The arithmetic all holds; it's the speech's figure that's off.
pointed: One way to check a figure like this is to imagine a round number of travellers and count how many land in each group.

discrimination.goal: Understand how the PC algorithm finds the skeleton of a causal graph

part.title: Edge removal in the skeleton phase
part.note: How PC deletes edges using conditional independence tests over growing conditioning sets

concepts.label: Searching neighbour subsets of growing size

discrimination.log: PC starts from a complete graph and removes edges when a conditional independence test says two variables are independent given some set.
discrimination.summary: For sizes k = 0, 1, 2, ..., PC tests each remaining adjacent pair X, Y against subsets of size k of X's current neighbours (minus Y). The first subset that makes them independent removes the edge for good and is stored as the separating set. Neighbourhoods shrink as edges go, which keeps the search small.
discrimination.understanding: PC's skeleton phase: start from the complete undirected graph. For k = 0, 1, 2, ... and each remaining adjacent pair X–Y, test X ⫫ Y | S for every S ⊆ adj(X) \ {Y} with |S| = k. If one test says independent, delete X–Y permanently and store S as sepset(X, Y); edges are never added back. adj(X) is the current neighbourhood, so it shrinks as edges are removed. The phase ends when no node has more than k neighbours left to condition on. Separating sets are later used to orient colliders: X – Z – Y with Z not in sepset(X, Y) becomes X → Z ← Y.

discrimination.goal: Fix a bug in a small Python inventory script

part.title: Default arguments
part.note: When Python evaluates default argument values and what that means for lists

discrimination.log: The inventory keeps items from earlier calls. I think it's the items=[] default.
discrimination.summary: Python evaluates default values once, when the def runs, so items=[] is one list shared by every call that uses the default. append mutates that shared list, so items pile up across calls. The fix is items=None and creating a new list inside the function.
discrimination.understanding: Default argument values are evaluated once, at function definition time, and stored on the function. A mutable default such as [] or {} is therefore one object shared by all calls that rely on the default. In-place operations (append, extend, item assignment) change that shared object, so state leaks between calls; rebinding the name (items = items + [x]) does not mutate it. The usual fix is a None default with `if items is None: items = []` inside the body. Passing a list explicitly avoids the shared default.

discrimination.goal: Understand d-separation well enough to read independence statements off a DAG

part.title: Colliders and conditioning
part.note: What conditioning on a collider or its descendant does to the path through it

discrimination.log: A collider is where two arrows meet head to head, like A → C ← B.
discrimination.summary: A path through a collider is blocked unless we condition on the collider or one of its descendants; then it opens. Chains and forks work the other way: they're open until we condition on the middle node.
discrimination.understanding: On a path, a non-collider (chain A → B → C or fork A ← B → C) is open unless conditioned on, and conditioning on it blocks the path. A collider (A → C ← B) blocks the path unless the collider itself or any of its descendants is in the conditioning set, which opens it. Two nodes are d-separated given Z when every path between them is blocked given Z. So A and B in A → C ← B are marginally independent but dependent given C, and also dependent given any descendant of C. Conditioning on a non-descendant of C does not open the path.

discrimination.goal: Write up the customer survey results for the quarterly review

part.title: Reporting percentages correctly
part.note: What each percentage in the survey write-up is out of

concepts.label: The base a percentage is out of

discrimination.log: Percentages should say who they're out of, and some questions let people pick several answers.
discrimination.summary: Each percentage is out of the people who answered that question, its base, which can be smaller than the whole sample. On multi-select questions the answers can add up to more than 100% because people pick several.
discrimination.understanding: A percentage only means something with its base: the people who were asked that question and answered it. Questions that were skipped or shown only to some respondents have smaller bases than the full sample, so their percentages can't be added to or directly compared with percentages on other bases. To turn a percentage into a count you multiply by that question's base, not the total sample. Single-select answers add up to 100% (up to rounding); multi-select answers usually add up to more, and a share of respondents is not a share of answers. Small bases (under about 30) give unstable percentages and should be flagged.

discrimination.goal: Plan the office move so it finishes before the lease ends

part.title: Scheduling dependent tasks
part.note: How long the move takes and which tasks can slip

concepts.label: Slack in tasks off the critical path

discrimination.log: Some tasks can happen at the same time, but the move itself has to wait for packing.
discrimination.summary: How long the project takes is set by the longest chain of tasks that depend on each other, the critical path. Tasks off that chain can slip a little without delaying the end; that's their slack.
discrimination.understanding: A task can start once every task it depends on has finished, so its earliest start is the latest earliest finish among them. The project's length is the longest path through the dependencies, the critical path; tasks on it have no slack. Parallel tasks don't add up: only the longest branch counts. A task's slack is how far it can slip without delaying the end, its latest start minus its earliest start. Shortening a task off the critical path doesn't shorten the project; shortening one on it can, until another path becomes the longest.

discrimination.goal: Study for the managerial finance exam on capital budgeting

part.title: Choosing projects with NPV and IRR
part.note: Deciding which investment projects to accept and comparing two projects

discrimination.log: NPV is the main rule; IRR can disagree with it when comparing projects.
discrimination.summary: NPV discounts all of a project's cash flows at the cost of capital and you accept projects with a positive NPV. IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero, and when choosing between mutually exclusive projects you should go with the higher NPV rather than the higher IRR.
discrimination.understanding: NPV is the sum of all cash flows, including the initial outlay at time 0, each discounted at the project's cost of capital; accept independent projects with NPV > 0. IRR is the rate at which NPV equals zero; for a conventional project (outflow then inflows) accepting when IRR exceeds the cost of capital gives the same decision as NPV. For mutually exclusive projects IRR can rank wrongly because of differences in scale or timing, so choose the one with the higher NPV; the crossover rate is where their NPV profiles cross. Non-conventional cash flows (sign changes more than once) can give several IRRs or none. IRR implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR, while NPV assumes the cost of capital. Common mistakes: forgetting to include or discount the time-0 outlay correctly (it is not discounted), discounting at the wrong rate, including sunk costs or financing costs in the cash flows, and comparing IRR to zero instead of to the cost of capital.

discrimination.goal: Estimate how much working capital the wholesaler needs for next year's treasury plan

part.title: Cash conversion cycle
part.note: How long cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers

discrimination.log: The cash cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days.
discrimination.summary: The cash conversion cycle is days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payables outstanding. A longer cycle means more cash is tied up in working capital, so growth needs more funding.
discrimination.understanding: The cash conversion cycle (CCC) = DIO + DSO − DPO: how many days pass between paying suppliers and collecting cash from customers. DIO = inventory / cost of goods sold × 365, and DPO = payables / cost of goods sold × 365 (purchases is also acceptable), while DSO = receivables / revenue × 365; using revenue for inventory or payables days, or COGS for receivables days, is a common error. Payable days are subtracted because supplier credit finances the cycle; adding them is the classic mistake. A longer CCC ties up more cash; the working capital needed is roughly the daily cost or sales volume times the days involved, so it grows with sales even if the days stay constant. Stretching payables shortens the cycle but may cost early-payment discounts or supplier goodwill. Year-end balances can be distorted by seasonality, so averages over the year are better for planning. A negative CCC (customers pay before suppliers are paid) is possible and means suppliers finance the business.

discrimination.goal: Write up the induction proof for the discrete maths problem set

part.title: Proof by induction
part.note: Proving a statement for every n from a starting value

concepts.label: Using the hypothesis in the inductive step

discrimination.log: Base case first, then assume it holds for n and show it for n + 1.
discrimination.summary: You show the statement holds for the first value, then show that if it holds for some n it also holds for n + 1. Together these give it for every n from the starting value on.
discrimination.understanding: An induction proof needs a base case at the value where the claim starts and an inductive step that works for every n from that value on. The base case must be checked at the real starting value: proving it at n = 1 doesn't cover a claim meant from n = 0, and proving a step without any base case proves nothing (a false claim like n = n + 1 has a valid-looking step). The step assumes the statement for n and derives it for n + 1; assuming the statement for n + 1, or working backwards from it without reversible steps, is circular. The step must actually use the hypothesis, and must hold for the smallest n too: the 'all horses are the same colour' argument fails because the step from n = 1 to n = 2 has no overlap between the two groups. Strong induction may assume all earlier cases, but if the step reaches back k values it needs k base cases. Checking several small cases, however many, is evidence, not a proof.

discrimination.goal: Set the weekly production mix for the bakery to maximise profit

part.title: Solving the production linear program
part.note: Choosing how many of each product to bake under oven-hour and flour limits

concepts.label: The optimum at a corner of the feasible region

discrimination.log: The best plan sits at a corner where the limits meet.
discrimination.summary: The plans that meet every limit form a polygon, and because profit is linear the best plan is at one of its corners. The limits that are used up exactly at that corner are the ones holding profit back.
discrimination.understanding: With a linear objective and linear constraints, if the feasible region is non-empty and the profit is bounded, an optimum occurs at a corner (vertex), so it is enough to compare the corners; if the profit line is parallel to an edge, every point on that edge ties. A corner is the intersection of two constraint lines that also satisfies every other constraint, including non-negativity; an intersection that breaks a third limit is not a candidate. Rounding a fractional optimum to whole units can make it infeasible or no longer optimal, so integer plans need checking separately. A constraint is binding if it holds with equality at the optimum; only binding constraints can have a non-zero shadow price, and a constraint with spare capacity has a shadow price of zero. The shadow price is the profit gained per extra unit of that resource, and it only holds within a range: beyond it the set of binding constraints changes. An empty feasible region or an unbounded profit means there is no optimal corner at all.

discrimination.goal: Finish the DC circuits problem set for the introductory electromagnetism course

part.title: Resistors in series and parallel
part.note: Equivalent resistance and the power each resistor dissipates

discrimination.log: Series resistors just add, parallel ones combine as reciprocals, and the current splits between parallel branches.
discrimination.summary: In series the resistances add and the same current flows through each; in parallel the reciprocals add, so the total is smaller than the smallest resistor, and each resistor has the full voltage across it. The power in each resistor follows from P = I²R or P = V²/R with that resistor's own current or voltage.
discrimination.understanding: Resistors in series carry the same current and their resistances add: R = R1 + R2 + …; the supply voltage divides between them in proportion to resistance. Resistors in parallel share the same voltage and their conductances add: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …, so the equivalent is always smaller than the smallest branch, and two equal resistors R in parallel give R/2. A common mistake is to add parallel resistances directly, or to compute 1/R1 + 1/R2 and forget to invert the result. The power in a resistor is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, using that resistor's own current and voltage, not the supply's; applying V²/R with the full supply voltage to one resistor in a series chain is a frequent error. In series the larger resistor dissipates more power (same I, P = I²R); in parallel the smaller resistor dissipates more (same V, P = V²/R). The total power equals the sum of the individual powers, and equals V_supply²/R_equivalent, which is a good consistency check. Ammeters go in series and voltmeters in parallel with the element they measure.

discrimination.goal: Pick the motor for the cooling-water pump before the purchase order goes out

part.title: Pump power
part.note: Working out the hydraulic power and the shaft power the motor must supply

concepts.label: Hydraulic power from flow and head

discrimination.log: Power is flow times head times ρg, and the pump isn't perfect so the motor has to supply more.
discrimination.summary: The power given to the water is ρ·g·Q·H, with Q the volume flow and H the head the pump must provide. Because the pump loses some energy, the shaft power is the hydraulic power divided by the pump efficiency.
discrimination.understanding: Hydraulic power is P = ρ·g·Q·H, equivalently Δp·Q, with ρ in kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², Q in m³/s and H in metres; flows given in L/s must be divided by 1000 and flows in m³/h by 3600, and unit slips here are the most common error. H is the total head the pump must supply: the static lift plus the friction and fitting losses in the pipework (and any pressure difference between the two ends), not the static lift alone. Shaft power is the hydraulic power divided by the pump efficiency, never multiplied by it, so shaft power is always larger; electrical input is shaft power divided again by the motor efficiency. For example 10 L/s of water against a 25 m head is 1000 × 9.81 × 0.010 × 25 = 2.45 kW of hydraulic power, and at 70% pump efficiency the shaft needs about 3.5 kW. The motor is then chosen as the next standard size above the shaft power at the duty point, with some margin, and checked at the pump's maximum-power operating point. The fluid's own density matters: using 1000 kg/m³ for a glycol mix or oil gives the wrong power.

discrimination.goal: Prepare for the genetics exam on dihybrid crosses and linkage

part.title: Dihybrid crosses and linked genes
part.note: Expected offspring ratios for two genes, and how linkage changes them

discrimination.log: Two genes on different chromosomes give 9:3:3:1, but linked genes mess that up.
discrimination.summary: When two genes are on different chromosomes they assort independently, so crossing two double heterozygotes gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio and a testcross gives 1:1:1:1. If the genes are linked, the parental combinations show up more often than expected, and the share of recombinant offspring is the recombination frequency.
discrimination.understanding: For two unlinked genes with complete dominance, AaBb × AaBb gives phenotypes in 9:3:3:1, and the testcross AaBb × aabb gives 1:1:1:1; the testcross is the cleaner way to measure linkage because each offspring's phenotype shows the gamete it got from the heterozygote. Linked genes on the same chromosome are inherited together unless a crossover separates them, so in a testcross the two parental classes are the most common and the two recombinant classes are the rarest. Recombination frequency = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring, and it never exceeds 50%, because a value of 50% is indistinguishable from independent assortment. Which classes are parental depends on the heterozygote's phase: in coupling (AB/ab) the parentals are AB and ab, in repulsion (Ab/aB) they are Ab and aB, so you identify parentals by their high counts, not by assuming AB is parental. One map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to 1% recombination, and map distances from two-point crosses are roughly additive only for short distances because double crossovers go undetected. A common mistake is to compute recombination frequency from an F2 (AaBb × AaBb) as if it were a testcross, or to divide recombinants by the number of parental offspring rather than by the total. Another is to treat a deviation from 9:3:3:1 as linkage without checking it is larger than chance, for example with a chi-square test.

discrimination.goal: Write the plate-count section of tomorrow's QC report on the fermentation broth

part.title: Viable counts from serial dilutions
part.note: Working back from colonies on a plate to CFU per mL of the original broth

concepts.label: CFU per mL from a plate count

discrimination.log: Each tube is 1:10, so I multiply the colony count back up by the dilution and the volume plated.
discrimination.summary: In a serial dilution the dilution factors multiply, so three 1:10 steps give a 10^-3 dilution. To get CFU per mL of the original sample you divide the colony count by the dilution and by the volume plated in mL, using a plate in the countable range.
discrimination.understanding: In a serial dilution each step's factor is the volume transferred divided by the total volume after transfer, so 100 µL into 900 µL is 1:10 but 100 µL into 1 mL is 1:11; the cumulative dilution is the product of the step factors, not their sum. CFU/mL of the original sample = colonies ÷ (cumulative dilution × volume plated in mL); for example 45 colonies from 0.1 mL of the 10^-6 tube is 45 ÷ (10^-6 × 0.1) = 4.5 × 10^8 CFU/mL. Forgetting to divide by the plated volume (when it isn't 1 mL) is a common error that gives an answer 10-fold too low for a 0.1 mL spread plate. Only plates in the countable range, usually 30–300 colonies, are used: plates above it are too crowded (TNTC) and plates below it are statistically unreliable. Counts are reported as colony-forming units, not cells, because clumps or chains grow into a single colony, so plate counts usually underestimate cell numbers. Results are reported in scientific notation with two significant figures, and duplicate plates at the same dilution are averaged before the calculation. A consistency check is that a plate at the next 10-fold dilution should have roughly a tenth of the colonies.

discrimination.goal: Write the essay on whether knowledge is justified true belief for the epistemology seminar

part.title: Gettier cases and the JTB analysis
part.note: What Gettier's counterexamples show about the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge

discrimination.log: Gettier's examples have someone with a justified true belief who still doesn't seem to know.
discrimination.summary: The traditional analysis says you know p when p is true, you believe p, and you're justified in believing it. Gettier's cases show someone meeting all three conditions without knowing, so the three conditions aren't sufficient for knowledge.
discrimination.understanding: The JTB analysis says S knows that p if and only if p is true, S believes p, and S is justified in believing p. Gettier (1963) gave cases in which all three conditions hold but the subject intuitively doesn't know, because the belief is true by luck: Smith justifiably infers 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket' from false evidence about Jones, and the belief is true only because Smith himself, unknowingly, gets the job and has ten coins. Gettier cases target the sufficiency of the three conditions, not their necessity: they don't show that truth, belief or justification is unnecessary for knowledge. A common mistake is to describe the subject's belief as false or unjustified; in a genuine Gettier case it is both true and justified, which relies on justification being fallible (one can be justified in a false belief, e.g. the belief about Jones). Another mistake is to say Gettier showed knowledge can't be defined; he showed only that JTB as stated isn't sufficient, and responses add a fourth condition (no false lemmas, defeasibility) or replace justification (reliabilism, safety). Gettier didn't propose the JTB analysis himself; he attributed versions of it to Plato, Chisholm and Ayer. Fake-barn cases (Goldman 1976, crediting Ginet) are a later variant in which the luck comes from the environment rather than from a false premise.

discrimination.goal: Reconstruct the eligibility argument in the housing-policy brief for the council committee

part.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions
part.note: What the brief's eligibility rules require and what they guarantee

discrimination.log: The brief keeps saying residency 'qualifies' people, but I think the rule only says you can't qualify without it.
discrimination.summary: A necessary condition is one you can't qualify without; a sufficient condition is one that guarantees you qualify. 'Only residents qualify' makes residency necessary, not sufficient.
discrimination.understanding: A is sufficient for B when A guarantees B ('if A then B'); A is necessary for B when B can't hold without A ('if B then A', equivalently 'if not A then not B'). 'Only residents qualify' and 'you qualify only if you are a resident' both make residency necessary for qualifying, not sufficient; 'if you are a resident, you qualify' makes it sufficient. The commonest mistake is reading 'only if' as 'if', which reverses the direction of the conditional. From a necessary condition you may infer that someone who lacks it doesn't qualify, but not that someone who has it does; inferring that is affirming the consequent. Likewise, from a sufficient condition you may infer that someone who has it qualifies, but not that someone who lacks it doesn't; that is denying the antecedent. 'B unless A' means 'if not A then B', and 'not B unless A' makes A necessary for B. A condition can be necessary without being sufficient (residency, when income is also tested), sufficient without being necessary, or both ('if and only if'), and several necessary conditions can be jointly sufficient even when none is sufficient alone.

# Serial dilution plan for E. coli plate counts

For Thursday's run. The overnight culture is expected at about 1 × 10^9 CFU/mL.

## Diluent

Make 10 mL of 1× PBS from the 10× stock: 1 mL of 10× PBS plus 10 mL of sterile water.

## Dilution series

Each step: 100 µL of the previous tube into 900 µL of 1× PBS, a 1:10 dilution.
Six steps take the culture from undiluted to 10^-6.
Plating 100 µL of the 10^-6 tube should give about 100 colonies (1 × 10^9 × 10^-6 × 0.1 mL).

## Counting

Count only plates with 30–300 colonies.
CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (dilution × volume plated in mL).

Plating 100 µL of the 10^-6 tube should give about 100 colonies (1 × 10^9 × 10^-6 × 0.1 mL).

# Field report: snail population at Pond B

BIO 214 ecology practical, group 3.

## Methods

On day 1 we caught 60 snails, marked each shell with a dot of waterproof paint, and released them where we found them.
On day 3 we caught 80 snails, of which 12 were marked.

## Results

Lincoln–Petersen estimate: N = (60 × 80) ÷ 12 = 400 snails.
This assumes the population is closed between samples, marks are not lost, and marked snails mix evenly back into the population.

## Discussion

The pond margin we sampled covers 200 m², so the density is about 4 snails per m².

concepts.label: The asymmetry of verification and falsification

checks.file:
# Does the problem of induction undermine science?

## 2. Popper's response

Hume argued that no number of observed cases logically entails a universal generalisation: past regularities don't guarantee future ones.
Popper accepted this and concluded that science does not rely on induction at all.
His key point is an asymmetry between verification and falsification.
No finite set of observations can verify 'All swans are white', however many white swans we see.
But one accepted observation of a black swan falsifies it, by modus tollens: if all swans are white, this swan is white; this swan is not white; so not all swans are white.
On Popper's view, then, a theory that survives many severe tests has thereby been shown to be probably true.

## 3. An objection

The Duhem-Quine problem complicates this: a failed prediction refutes the theory together with its auxiliary assumptions, so logic alone does not say which to give up.
added: His key point is an asymmetry between verification and falsification.
No finite set of observations can verify 'All swans are white', however many white swans we see.
But one accepted observation of a black swan falsifies it, by modus tollens: if all swans are white, this swan is white; this swan is not white; so not all swans are white.
checks.other_bug: Line 10 says that on Popper's view a theory surviving severe tests is shown to be probably true; Popper denied this. Surviving tests only corroborates a theory, and he held that corroboration is not inductive confirmation or probability of truth.

concepts.label: Disclosure of purpose, procedures and risks

checks.file:
# Ethics committee assessment: memory and attention study (proposal 2026-14)

Reviewer: second reader, social and behavioural panel.

## Review level

Committee rule 4.2: every study that poses more than minimal risk needs full-board review.
This study poses minimal risk, so rule 4.2 shows that it does not need full-board review.

## Consent

The information sheet states the study's purpose, that participants complete a 40-minute online memory task, and that the only foreseeable risk is mild fatigue.
Recruitment is through a university-wide mailing list rather than by the investigator in her own classes, so students are not asked to take part by someone who grades them.
The sheet says participants may withdraw at any time without giving a reason, and that withdrawing will not affect their course credit or payment for time already spent.

## Recommendation

Approve, subject to the minor wording changes listed in the annex.

Recruitment is through a university-wide mailing list rather than by the investigator in her own classes, so students are not asked to take part by someone who grades them.
